title: Beyond the Harness: A Journey Towards Adaptative Engineering - Rajiv Chandegra, Annicha Labs

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core thesis is rethinking agent harness architecture from fixed predetermined structures to adaptive, emergent multi-agent self-organizing systems. The design philosophy applies cross-domain to any agent system rather than a specific application vertical. The talk covers both design-time constraint selection and runtime emergence and adaptation of the harness. The talk assumes familiarity with existing AI harnesses and draws on complexity science, systems theory, and philosophy. This is a single-speaker presentation delivered at the AI Engineer conference. All supporting evidence consists of direct quotes from the transcript.

summary: Rajiv Chandegra, a practicing medical doctor and director of Annicha Labs, presents adaptive engineering as a new design philosophy for AI engineering. The current paradigm uses fixed, predetermined harnesses — system prompts, agents.md files, tool calling, specialized agents — configured before runtime, producing reliable, auditable, linearly causal outputs analogous to Taylorism or a factory assembly line. This works for complicated problems (like building a jumbo jet) that are hard but knowable and predictable. However, Chandegra distinguishes complicated from complex problems: complex systems (flocks, markets, organizations) have parts that constantly interact and adapt, so the whole cannot be derived from analyzing parts. Treating complex problems as complicated ones is a critical and expensive mistake. Complex systems require diverse agents interacting locally, learning recursively, and producing emergence — novel patterns no single part designed. These systems settle into attractors (stable states) while remaining self-organizing with no central steering. Chandegra defines adaptive engineering as designing constraints so the harness emerges on its own, stabilizes, and adapts at runtime in ways impossible to specify in advance. The harness becomes an ongoing output rather than a predetermined input. The engineer dictates constraints — three key questions frame this: enable agents more or govern them with guardrails; reward coherence toward a goal or cost divergence outside a container; and control the speed or rate of coupling. The emergent harness can only be sensed and responded to, not hard-edited. Chandegra identifies major failure modes: attractors that feel stable but aren't optimal, lack of genuine selection pressure causing drift, monoculture risk from identical training data, legibility collapse, and loss of pre-runtime predictability. He emphasizes neither approach is better — they are different philosophies on a continuum. His takeaway: as models improve exponentially and AI engineering moves into the real world (physical space, multi-agent, multi-human, cross-institutional), the limiting factor will no longer be model strength but harness adaptability, defined as decentralized multi-agent orchestration that adapts mid-runtime.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Complicated problems (jumbo jets, clocks) are decomposable and predictable; complex problems (flocks, markets, organizations) have interacting, adapting parts whose whole cannot be derived from analysis of parts.
Treating complex problems as complicated ones is one of the most expensive mistakes in modern design and engineering, causing failure not from poor execution but from miscategorization.

Adaptive engineering is the discipline of designing constraints so the harness emerges, stabilizes, and adapts at runtime in ways impossible to specify in advance; the harness becomes output, not input.

The engineer's role shifts to dictating constraints — enabling vs governing, rewarding coherence vs costing divergence, controlling coupling speed — and sensing and responding to the emergent harness rather than hard-editing it.
Fixed and adaptive engineering exist on a continuum, not as a binary choice; neither is better, they are different design philosophies for different use cases.

Adaptive engineering faces real failure modes: suboptimal attractors, drift without genuine selection pressure, monoculture from identical training data, legibility collapse, and loss of pre-runtime predictability.
As models improve exponentially and AI enters the real world, the limiting factor will be harness adaptability — decentralized multi-agent orchestration that adapts mid-runtime — not model strength.

Horizontal intelligence (group coordination) is more adaptive and higher-leverage than vertical intelligence (individual agent improvement); runtime adaptivity, not design-time adaptivity, defines adaptive engineering.

sections.title: Introduction and Thesis
sections.summary: Rajiv introduces himself as a medical doctor and AI engineer at Annicha Labs, and states his thesis: the future of AI engineering must move beyond fixed static harnesses toward adaptive engineering.

sections.title: Current AI Engineering Paradigm: Fixed Harnesses
sections.summary: Describes the current paradigm where harnesses (system prompts, agents.md, tool calling, specialized agents, loop engineering) are predetermined before runtime. Lists common harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, LangChain, Hermes, Klein, Goose) and their properties: reliable, auditable, linear causality — analogous to Taylorism or a factory assembly line.

sections.title: Limitations of Fixed Harnesses and the Pivot to the Real World
sections.summary: Explains that reliability is bought by suppressing variance, creating a hard ceiling on novelty. Models accelerating makes harnesses quickly obsolete. Real-world exposure (multi-agent, multi-human, multi-institutional, physical) makes fixed harnesses brittle, requiring constant patching. Introduces adaptive engineering where the harness emerges and adapts mid-engineering.

sections.title: Philosophical Foundations: Reductionist vs. Relational Paradigms
sections.summary: Contrasts the reductionist/analytical view (world as stable parts with secondary relationships — metaphysics of factories and software) with the systems/relational view (processes and relationships come first; stable things are slow patterns in ongoing flows). Illustrates emergence with water's wetness and bird flocking. Cites Russell Ackoff's concept of a mess as dynamic tangles of problems in motion, explaining why fixed-harness engineering struggles with real-world scenarios.

sections.title: Complicated vs. Complex Problems
sections.summary: Distinguishes complicated problems (jumbo jet, clock — passive parts, decomposable, predictable, knowable) from complex problems (flock of birds, market, organization — parts constantly interacting and adapting, whole cannot be derived from parts). Complex systems require probe-sense-respond, not analyze-and-plan. Treating complex problems as complicated is identified as one of the most expensive mistakes in modern design and engineering.

sections.title: Ingredients of Complex Systems and Emergence
sections.summary: Details the ingredients of complex systems: diverse agents (not clones), local interaction (no agent sees the whole), recursive learning and adapting, and constant movement in response to everything. Emergence produces novel patterns no single part designed. Systems settle into attractors (stable states like water at room temperature), creating tension between constant local change and stable system-level patterns. Crucially, nobody steers — it is self-organizing.

sections.title: Defining Adaptive Engineering
sections.summary: Formally introduces adaptive engineering: designing constraints so the harness emerges on its own, stabilizes, and adapts as needed in response to changing environments in ways impossible to specify in advance. The harness becomes ongoing output rather than input. Agents create the harness as birds create the flock — the engineer no longer builds it but lets agents form the harness that best fits the environment in that moment.

sections.title: Simulation of Emergent Harness Formation
sections.summary: Describes a simulation: undifferentiated but capable agents interact, coupling builds until roughly one connection per agent, and a system emerges. The engineer's lever becomes the rate of coupling. Agents specialize into niches as environmental pressure amplifies small differences; identity becomes relative position, not something assigned. Agents stop connecting randomly, form clusters, and the system draws boundaries. Conventions and governance emerge spontaneously without central authority, enabling decentralized adaptation.

sections.title: The Engineer's Relocated Role and the Continuum
sections.summary: Adaptive engineering does not abolish the engineer but relocates emphasis: the engineer dictates constraints (rules of the game), gives agents space to explore, and senses and responds to the emergent harness rather than restarting. Fixed and adaptive engineering exist on a continuum, not as a binary; each suits different use cases.

sections.title: Distinctions from Existing Harnesses: Horizontal vs. Vertical Intelligence
sections.summary: Distinguishes Hermes AI's vertical intelligence (making individual agents smarter) from horizontal intelligence (how groups of agents coordinate), arguing horizontal is more adaptive, agile, and higher-leverage. Contrasts Pi's design-time adaptivity (malleable, extensible, customizable at preparation stage) with runtime adaptivity (system self-reorganizes while running), which defines adaptive engineering. Pi is a strong example of the former but not yet a self-organizing multi-agent system.

sections.title: Engineering Constraints, Failure Modes, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Details the constraint-design questions: enable vs govern agents, reward coherence vs cost divergence, and control coupling speed. The emergent harness can only be sensed and responded to, not hard-edited. Compares factory vs adaptive philosophies — neither better, different use cases; control is decentralized in adaptive. Lists failure modes: suboptimal attractors, drift without genuine selection pressure, monoculture from identical training data, legibility collapse, and loss of pre-runtime predictability. Concludes that as models improve exponentially and AI enters the real world, the limiting factor becomes harness adaptability — decentralized multi-agent orchestration adapting mid-runtime — not model strength. Calls for community engagement.

demonstrations: Water's wetness as an emergent property not present in constituent oxygen and hydrogen
Bird flocking arising from three simple local rules with no single bird containing the flock
Jumbo jet as a complicated problem: hard but decomposable, predictable, knowable
Agents coupling from undifferentiated state until roughly one connection per agent, then system emerges
Two redundant agents diverging into niches as environmental pressure amplifies small differences
Emergent clusters with boundaries drawn by the system, not the engineer, leading to spontaneous conventions and governance
limitations: Fixed harnesses become brittle when exposed to dynamic, messy real-world scenarios involving multi-agent, multi-human, cross-institutional, and physical-world interactions
Fixed harnesses require constant human patching for unanticipated situations, eventually becoming more complicated than the actual problem
Reliability of fixed harnesses is bought by suppressing variance, placing a hard ceiling on novelty
Treating complex problems as complicated ones causes failure from miscategorization, not poor execution
Central authority in harness design leads to brittleness in changing environments
Adaptive engineering can settle into suboptimal attractors that feel stable but aren't the best solution
Without genuine selection pressure, adaptive systems drift rather than improve
Monoculture risk: agents trained on the same data lack genuine diversity
Legibility collapses as adaptability increases — complex systems cannot be easily pinned down or explained
No predictability ahead of runtime because the system is constantly moving

organization.name: Annicha Labs
organization.summary: Annicha Labs is a London healthcare and life-sciences technology company and research lab. Its homepage and about page describe deep research, strategic advisory, and product innovation aimed at the next 100 years of human flourishing, including a post-AI future of multi-agents in contact with physical and social worlds. The live services surface is Strategic Advisory (including AI Capabilities), Ventures, and The Gateway. Rajiv Chandegra, a practicing London physician, is director/CEO and presented adaptive engineering from this affiliation. Site copyright is Annicha Group Limited.
